newsitem.title: USA: Senate race in Oregon hinges on absentee ballots.
newsitem.headline: Senate race in Oregon hinges on absentee ballots.

text.p: Republican Gordon Smith was leading the nation's final undecided Senate race Wednesday but a winner had not yet been declared with more than 400,000 absentee ballots yet to be counted.

With 92 percent of precincts reporting, Smith had a 15,000-vote lead, 49 percent of the total, compared with 47 percent for Democrat Tom Bruggere. "We expect that margin to hold," Smith spokesman Dan Lavey said.

But he said Smith probably would not declare victory until Thursday at the earliest and television networks said the race was too close to call because 40 percent of the state's 2 million voters had requested absentee ballots.

Voters had until the polls closed Tuesday to get their ballots in and officials then faced the arduous task of manually comparing absentee ballots and polling place books to eliminate possible double-voting.

In Multnomah County, the state's largest with 20 percent of the electorate, more than 100,000 people turned in absentee ballots and officials did not expect to begin counting them until Thursday. Some results were expected to be available late Wednesday from the key suburban Portland counties of Clackamas and Washington.

Oregon's Democratic Gov. John Kitzhaber last year vetoed a bill that would have eliminated voting booths in the state in favour of mail elections but proponents of the move, including Secretary of State Phil Kiesling, were likely to try again.
"It would seem most efficacious to do it all by mail rather than have this double-headed, awkard and expensive system," state elections manager Fred Neal said.
Absentee ballots can be had for the asking in Oregon, which conducted the nation's first congressional vote-by-mail election this year.
